title: Continuous GPS updates disclose precise location and movement patterns
description: The child sends live GPS coordinates at regular intervals to the backend. This flow directly reveals highly sensitive location data, enabling inference of current whereabouts, routines, home/school locations, and movement history if the data is observed in transit or processed without adequate minimization.

title: Regular location reports enable linkability of multiple observations to the same child
description: Because GPS coordinates are transmitted at regular intervals from the same child's device to the backend, separate messages can be linked together into a continuous trace. Even if direct identifiers are minimized, timing, route continuity, device/session metadata, or stable tokens can make successive reports linkable to one child over time.
assumptions: The backend can correlate recurring submissions using network metadata, session identifiers, device identifiers, or trajectory continuity.
uncertainty_note: Applicable linkability threat is clear, but exact threat-tree sub-node id may differ by LINDDUN Pro edition.

title: Location stream enables identification of the child
description: Live GPS coordinates, especially when frequent and precise, can identify the child by revealing unique places such as home, school, or regular activity locations. If the backend associates the stream with an account, device, or guardian profile, the child's identity becomes directly inferable from this flow.

uncertainty_note: Identification risk is strong for precise child geolocation, though exact sub-node id is based on best judgement.

If storing every ping is not strictly necessary for the service purpose, this write creates avoidable explicit disclosure into persistent storage beyond the minimality principle.

title: Backend may be unable to prove who granted or accepted secondary-guardian access
description: If the system lacks strong audit trails for invitation, acceptance, and access-grant events, the parties could later dispute whether the secondary guardian was legitimately authorized to receive the child's live location. This weakens accountability around a sensitive disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes insufficient logging, timestamps, actor binding, or evidence of consent/acceptance for the access grant.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation is plausible for the access-grant aspect of this flow, but whether it is material depends on the actual audit design.

title: Partner-shared analytics may enable cross-context linkage
description: Even if the backend sends only aggregated usage and engagement analytics, recurring reports segmented by cohort, campaign, region, device type, or time window can act as stable fingerprints. The advertising/analytics partner may link these datasets with its own identifiers or other customer datasets, enabling linkage of app-user groups or, in edge cases, small segments back to individuals.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics include breakdowns or repeated dimensions that remain stable over time, and that the partner has other datasets to correlate against.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on best judgment rather than a retrieved threat-tree excerpt; exact node label may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Aggregated engagement analytics may still disclose user interests or behavior patterns
description: Usage and engagement analytics can reveal sensitive behavioral patterns such as feature adoption, session timing, content/topic affinity, or monetization behavior. Even in aggregate form, disclosures about small cohorts or niche features may expose sensitive characteristics of the underlying users to the partner.
assumptions: Assumes analytics contain sufficiently granular dimensions or small-group reporting such that sensitive inferences about users or user groups are possible.
uncertainty_note: Exact disclosure sub-node is chosen by best judgment because the provided context did not include threat-tree details.

title: Partner may use analytics for purposes beyond users' reasonable expectations
description: Users may expect app telemetry to support service operation, but not necessarily sharing with an advertising/analytics partner to fund the free tier. If the partner uses the received analytics for ad targeting, profiling, benchmarking, model training, or combining with data from other clients, the processing can become unaware or unexpected from the user's perspective.
assumptions: Assumes users are not clearly informed that their usage analytics are shared with an external advertising/analytics partner for monetization-related purposes.
uncertainty_note: Threat applies strongly at the receiving party, but the exact U sub-node may differ depending on the project's LINDDUN Pro tree version.

title: Sharing analytics with an ad/analytics partner may lack a valid legal basis or exceed purpose limitation
description: Sending usage and engagement analytics to a third-party advertising/analytics partner for funding the free tier can conflict with consent, transparency, purpose-limitation, and data-minimization requirements, especially if the data are not truly anonymous. If users have not validly consented or cannot object, the sharing may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics are personal data or reasonably re-identifiable/pseudonymous, and that consent/notice/opt-out controls may be insufficient for this third-party sharing.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on jurisdiction, contract terms, and whether the shared dataset is truly anonymous; exact node chosen by best judgment.

title: Backend can identify the child from SOS/check-in content and account context
description: The flow carries a manual SOS/check-in together with current location from the child to the backend. Even if the child is represented by an app account or device identifier rather than a real name in this flow, the backend can single out and identify the child by combining the message, location, account/session metadata, and device/network context.
assumptions: The backend receives or can derive a stable account, device, or session identifier for the sender, and stores or processes the message in a way that distinguishes one child from others.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-judgement for identifiability at the receiving process; exact sub-node labeling may vary between LINDDUN Pro catalogs.

title: Backend can link repeated check-ins and SOS events to the same child over time
description: Manual check-ins and SOS messages with location are highly linkable. The backend can correlate repeated submissions using account identifiers, device identifiers, timestamps, route patterns, and location history, building a longitudinal profile of the child's movements and behavior.
assumptions: The service retains identifiers or metadata across sessions/events, allowing multiple events to be associated with the same child.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro sub-node id for linkability may differ; node selected by best judgement.

title: Sensitive location disclosure to backend operators or unauthorized backend recipients
description: This flow discloses the child's current location and the fact that they initiated a check-in or SOS. That reveals highly sensitive personal data, potentially including whereabouts, routines, and emergency status, to the backend and anyone with access to backend-side logs, analytics, support tooling, or compromised processing environments.
assumptions: Location and event content are visible in backend processing, storage, logs, or operational tooling beyond the minimum needed for delivery to the parent.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen as a generic disclosure-at-receiver threat; exact catalog numbering may vary.

title: Backend can detect the child's presence, activity, and possibly co-location from incoming SOS/check-in events
description: Receiving a manual check-in or SOS with current location lets the backend detect that the child is active at a specific time and place. Over multiple events, the backend may infer attendance at school, home presence, travel patterns, or co-location with other people or devices.
assumptions: The backend observes timestamps and sufficiently precise location data, and either stores events or can analyze them operationally.
uncertainty_note: Sub-node is a best-judgement fit for detectability/presence inference from event observation.

title: Location/event semantics enable inference of unawareness or vulnerability of the child
description: From the SOS/check-in content and location, the backend may infer intimate facts not explicitly provided, such as daily routines, school attendance, home address, likely age group, times when the child is unsupervised, or situations indicating distress or vulnerability. These inferences go beyond the child's likely expectation when simply sending a safety message.
assumptions: The backend has access to historical or contextual data enabling inference, or personnel/algorithms can interpret the location and timing semantics.
uncertainty_note: This is a best-judgement application of unawareness/non-transparent inference; exact fit depends on whether the system meaningfully informs users about such secondary inferences.

title: Collection of precise child location and emergency-status data may exceed necessity or valid consent expectations
description: A manual check-in/SOS flow necessarily involves sensitive child data, but the backend may collect, retain, or further use more than is necessary for immediate parent notification, such as precise coordinates, detailed metadata, or long retention of emergency events. If users are not given a clear legal basis, granular consent, or age-appropriate notice, this creates non-compliance risk.
assumptions: The service may retain or repurpose event/location data beyond immediate transmission, and compliance obligations for children's data and location data apply.
uncertainty_note: This is a compliance/privacy-engineering threat inferred from the flow and child/location context; exact applicability depends on jurisdiction, consent model, and retention/processing design.

title: Child may be unable to later deny or contest having sent a specific SOS/check-in
description: If the backend stores the event with account, device, timestamp, and location metadata, it may create strong evidence that a specific child sent a particular check-in or SOS. This can undermine plausible deniability, especially if messages were triggered under pressure, by mistake, or by someone else using the child's device.
assumptions: The backend logs and preserves message provenance and associated metadata in a way that can be attributed back to the child.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation/privacy relevance depends on whether preserving attributable evidence is unnecessary or harmful in this context.
